desc:
Consider the sums of all non-empty contiguous subarrays of nums. Two different subarrays (different start or end index) are counted separately even when their sums are equal.

Return the k largest of these sums in non-increasing order. All numbers in nums are positive.

nums = [3, 1, 2], k = 4
subarray sums: 6 (3,1,2), 4 (3,1), 3 (1,2), 3 (3), 2 (2), 1 (1)
answer = [6, 4, 3, 3]
hints: There are about n<sup>2</sup>/2 subarrays, far too many to sort when n is 3,000 and k is small. Which subarray has the largest sum?
Because every number is positive, shrinking a subarray from either end strictly lowers its sum. So the second largest sum is one of the two subarrays obtained from the full array by dropping an end.

Run a best-first search: keep a max-heap of candidate subarrays keyed by sum, starting from the whole array. Pop the best, record it, and push its two shrunk neighbours [l+1, r] and [l, r-1] (use a visited set so a subarray is never pushed twice).
editorial: Subarrays form a lattice: shrinking by one element at either end gives smaller sums. Every subarray other than the full array can be reached by shrinking some subarray with a larger sum, so the next largest sum is always the sum of an unvisited neighbour of an already-popped subarray.

Compute prefix sums so any subarray sum costs O(1). Start the heap with the full array. Repeat k times: pop the largest-sum subarray (l, r), append its sum to the answer, and push (l+1, r) and (l, r-1) when valid and not yet seen. The seen set matters because (l+1, r-1) can be reached from two parents.

Each pop pushes at most two entries, so the heap never exceeds 2k elements and the running time is O(n + k log k) with O(k) memory beyond the prefix sums. This 'pop and expand neighbours' pattern is the same one used for K Smallest Pair Sums.
